say: Today we are going to find every pair of numbers that joins to make 10. These pairs are called number bonds.
Then we will use them to make 20. And we will find out what the equals sign really means.
I have 10 counters. Watch carefully. [Show all 10. Hide some under the cup.] There are 6 counters I can still see. How many are under the cup?
How do you know? Say it as a number bond: “6 and __ make 10.”
How many different ways do you think there are to make 10 with two numbers? Guess, and write it down.
stuck: Stuck: start with all red counters. That is 10 + 0. Now change one to yellow.
Not sure if 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 are different: flip your ten-frame upside down and look.
For pairs who want more: use your bonds of 10 to make bonds of 20 (16 + 4).

say: “Let me list them in order: 0 + 10, 1 + 9, 2 + 8. What do you notice? The first number goes up by 1 and the second goes down by 1. That is how I know I have them all.”
“Now 20. I know 6 + 4 = 10. So 16 + 4 = 20. The ones stay the same. Only the tens change.”
“Look at 6 + 2 = 5 + __. Imagine a see-saw. Both sides must balance. 6 + 2 is 8, so the other side must be 8. What goes with 5? 3. Check: 5 + 3 = 8.”

do: Ask: “Say 5 + 3 = 4 + __ like a see-saw. What does each side equal?”
Magic triangle: “Which numbers are the corners? Each corner is counted in two sides.”
Ask: “How do you know you have found all the pairs?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Work out the left side first. What is it?”
Hint 2: “Make the same amount with counters on both sides of the see-saw.”
Hint 3: “Try the number 4 in the blank. Is the right side the same?”

say: “Mei says 4 + 4 = 8 + 1. Who agrees with Mei? How can we check?”
“What does the equals sign really mean?”
ask: “Mei says 4 + 4 = 8 + 1. Who agrees with Mei? How can we check?”
4 + 4 = 8 but 8 + 1 = 9, so Mei is wrong. The equals sign means both sides have the same value, not “the answer comes next”.

say: “You found every bond of 10 and you can say how you know you have them all. That is explaining why.”

l2-title.note: Objective: Know the bonds of 10, use them to find bonds of 20, balance equations, and reason about missing numbers. Materials: Ten-frames, red and yellow counters, a cup, a paper triangle with 6 circles. Online: Slide ten-frame with a hidden-counter reveal; each child uses 10 coins or paper pieces of two colours. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8 (game 2 to 6, quick questions 6 to 8; ask questions 1 to 3, and 4 and 5 only if you are on time), sneak-peek puzzles 8 to 12, explore 12 to 26, teaching 26 to 36 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36 to 40, worksheet 40 to 72 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (a 30-second stand-and-stretch reset after the page-1 check, taken from that slot; the last 6 minutes check page 2, after a 1-minute stand-up stretch), talk time 72 to 79, exit ticket 79 to 85, look-back 85 to 88, then flex time and goodbye 88 to 90 (this is the buffer: if you are behind, use it; do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose, any time or at home. Nobody is told which page they should be on.

l2-warm1.note: Minutes 2 to 6. Hidden counters: show 10 counters, hide some under a cup. How many are under the cup? Repeat with new splits.

l2-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Read each aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show. For 4 ask: "Can a number bond have 0 in it?" (yes: 10 + 0). Answers: 3, 8, 5, 0, 9. Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 6 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide.

l2-warmcheck.note: Minutes 8 to 12 (4 minutes). SAY (about 26 words, once): "Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked." Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone starts with a win. Question 2 makes you think. Children try both on their own paper (about a minute each). Then everyone answers ONCE, after the second question: face to face, each child keeps the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, children say the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). There are no private chat messages. Never use boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, and never read out or compare anyone's answer. Do not write scores down or announce them. Then click to show each answer to the whole group and say "Lots of us had a different idea, and that is fine." Look for good ideas to praise in a later lesson; do not keep a list of who found question 2 easy. When the worksheet starts (minute 40) invite the WHOLE group (“When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation”), never one child by name. Everyone joins Explore and the Mini-lesson. Answers: 1) 3. 7 + 3 = 10. 2) The same: 12 each. (7 + 5 = 12 and 6 + 6 = 12. Ali's 7 is 1 more than Mei's 6, but his 5 is 1 less than her 6.)

l2-explore1.note: Minutes 12 to 17. Pairs work with the materials: Ten-frames, red and yellow counters, a cup, a paper triangle with 6 circles. Pairs make 10 on a ten-frame with two colours in as many ways as they can and record each pair. Then ask: how do you know you have them all? Online: Slide ten-frame with a hidden-counter reveal; each child uses 10 coins or paper pieces of two colours. Go further (what-if) is on this slide from the start: any pair may choose it at any time, so nobody waits. The tutor does not choose who and does not announce it. Answers: 7 different pairs if 3 + 9 and 9 + 3 count as the same: 0 + 12, 1 + 11, 2 + 10, 3 + 9, 4 + 8, 5 + 7, 6 + 6. The first number goes up by 1 as the second goes down by 1.

l2-explore2.note: Minutes 17 to 26. Let pairs keep working and move around the room (or breakout rooms). Gather them to answer these. Answers: 1) 11 pairs from 0 + 10 to 10 + 0, or 6 different bonds if 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 are the same. 2) List in order: the first number goes up by 1 and the second goes down by 1. 3) It goes down by 1.

l2-teach1.note: Teach. Click to add each bond while children say it with you; show each on a ten-frame (red and yellow counters). Think-aloud: "Let me list them in order: 0 + 10, 1 + 9, 2 + 8. What do you notice? The first number goes up by 1 and the second goes down by 1. That is how I know I have them all." Then the summary: 11 bonds from 0 + 10 to 10 + 0, or 6 different pairs if 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 count as the same.

l2-try1.note: Children write on their own paper and say the answer together on three (online: nothing is held up to the camera). Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera. Then click. For c, ask how they found it: "the list goes 2 + 8 then 4 + 6, so 3 + 7 is missing".

l2-teach2.note: Click to build each row. Ask "What stays the same? What changes?" before revealing. Think-aloud: "I know 6 + 4 = 10. So 16 + 4 = 20. The ones stay the same. Only the tens change." Then the worked example at the bottom.

l2-try2.note: Own paper, ticked against the answer slide. For b: "1 + 9 = 10, so 11 + 9 = 20."

l2-teach3.note: Teach. Imagine a see-saw: both sides must balance. Ask first: "What do you think goes in the blank?" Many children say 8 because "the answer comes next". Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "6 + 2 is 8, so the other side must be 8. What goes with 5 to make 8? 3."

l2-key.note: Say the key ideas together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Reading "=" as "the answer comes next" (5 + 3 = 4 + __ answered 8). (2) Counting 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 as different pairs when asked for different pairs. (3) Magic triangle: trying numbers at random instead of thinking about the corners.

l2-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

l2-ws1.note: Minutes 40 to 50. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. At minute 40 read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then pairs read the rest. The workbook says: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group; invite the WHOLE group at once, for example: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

l2-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q2c: 0+10, 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5 are 6 different pairs if turned-round pairs count as the same. Reset (about 30 seconds, taken from this slot): when the answers are checked, everyone stands, reaches up high, shakes out their hands, takes one slow breath and sits down again, then page 2. Skip it if you are more than a minute behind.

l2-teachpage2.note: Teach before worksheet page 2, about 2 minutes in all (this slide replaces two separate slides). LEFT, magic triangle (Q5): here the target is 12, so the BIG numbers go in the corners. On the worksheet the target is 9: ask "Small sides... so which numbers should go in the corners?" but do not tell them. Click order: step 1, corners appear, step 2, step 3, the finished triangle. Check each side aloud: 4 + 3 + 5, 5 + 1 + 6, 6 + 2 + 4. RIGHT, two numbers (Q6): use real cubes. Take 2 cubes away and put them aside, share the rest into two equal towers, then add the 2 to one tower. Children who guess-and-check are fine too: ask them to check both clues.

l2-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who may need a short catch-up next lesson (never in front of the group).

l2-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q5: the corners 1, 2, 3 are given for 9 (small sides need small corners). Between 1 and 2: 6; between 2 and 3: 4; between 3 and 1: 5. For 10 the corners are 1, 3, 5 with 6, 2, 4 between. First, everyone stands up and stretches for about a minute (reach up high, touch your toes, shake out your hands) so there is some movement before talk time.

l2-stretch.note: For any pair that chooses to try more (these are on the slide only; Think harder T1 to T4 are in the workbook). Answers: 1) 10 and 16 (all three are 20). 2) 8 (20 − 4 = 16, and 8 + 8 = 16). 3) 6 pairs: 5 + 15, 6 + 14, 7 + 13, 8 + 12, 9 + 11, 10 + 10.

l2-challenge.note: For any pair that chooses Go further. Use it as a pair choice, or with volunteers in talk time (never call a child by name). Ask for the reason every time. Q3 is open: there is no single right answer, so ask children to check each other's work. Answers: 1) Circle 5, square 2 (2 × 5 + 2 = 12 and 5 + 2 × 2 = 9). One way to see it: the two totals differ by 3, and the only change is one circle swapped for one square, so a circle is 3 more than a square. Then 3 squares and 6 more make 12, so each square is 2. 2) Ben 7, Mei 4. (20 − 9 = 11 are shared; take away Ben's extra 3: 8, share 4 and 4; Ben has 4 + 3 = 7.) 3) Open. Yes, it still works. Totals 12, 13, 14 and 15 are possible. Example for 12: corners 2, 3, 4 with 7 between 2 and 3, 5 between 3 and 4 and 6 between 4 and 2.

l2-chdiag.note: Show this picture slide only if a pair asks for it, or is stuck on Go further. The pictures show each problem, not its answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Can you draw or build it? Do not point out the answer; wait for a child to find a pattern.

l2-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Reveal one answer at a time and ask a child to explain before you click. Many children stop at one answer: ask "Is there another way?" and "How do you know you found them all?" For Q3, ask two pairs to swap puzzles and solve each other's.

l2-talk.note: Minutes 72 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes. Then ask for volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"), never call a child by name to answer, and say that passing is always fine. No tallies and no rankings. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

l2-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 4 and 7. Extension: Make every side of the magic triangle total 11 (one way: corners 2, 4, 6 with 5, 1, 3 between them). Then ask: can every side total 13? No: the biggest possible side total is 12, with 4, 5, 6 in the corners.

l2-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88 (3 minutes, after the exit ticket). Children tick or write the Look-back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share their boxes. Praise the strategy ("Drawing it got you unstuck"), not the speed. The "Next time I will try" row is optional and is never marked; at the start of the next lesson the tutor may say, to the whole group, "Today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer" without naming anyone. Say: "Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. Then tick one thing you might try next time, if you like. You can pass." After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If the lesson ran late, finish whatever is still open (stamps, the look-back). If you are on time, say goodbye and thank the parents. Do not start anything new.
